newsitem.title: FRANCE: Troops rushed in after Paris rush-hour bomb.
newsitem.headline: Troops rushed in after Paris rush-hour bomb.

text.p: France rushed extra police and troops to major cities and border crossings on Wednesday after the bombing of a rush-hour Paris commuter train revived memories of last year's attacks by Algerian Moslem militants.

"Everything possible will be done to identify and punish those responsible for the attack," Prime Minister Alain Juppe told a hushed National Assembly, urging France to unite against "the blackmail of fear and violence".

Juppe said the blast bore striking similarities to the 1995 wave of bombings by Algerian Moslem rebels. Investigators have said the explosive mixture in Tuesday's crude bomb attack was identical to that used in last year's blasts.
Two people were killed and 88 others were wounded or left in shock by the bombing of the RER commuter train as it entered Port Royal underground station during Tuesday evening's rush hour.
Twenty-seven people were still in hospital on Wednesday night.
Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre said 1,800 soldiers were being assigned to assist police. Most would be deployed in Paris but many would help to tighten border controls, he said.
The bomb consisted of a 13 kg (29-lb) gas canister, Debre told a cabinet meeting. It was in a bag packed with nails.
"We must be alert to the possibility that this was not an isolated attack," said government spokesman Alain Lamassoure.
There were no immediate claims of responsibility, but the type of bomb, the target and the rush-hour timing recalled last year's attacks.

Moslem fundamentalist extremists fighting Algeria's French-backed military rulers claimed responsibility for those attacks, in which eight people were killed and more than 160 injured. The attacks began in July 1995 and ended in October.
Investigators said there had been several intelligence reports in recent weeks that Algerian Islamic guerrillas had arrived in France but these had not been confirmed.
The French daily Le Monde said a note by the DST counter-intelligence service last month reported that an Algerian Islamic extremist, living in Afghanistan, was planning an attack in France.

President Jacques Chirac and Juppe praised emergency workers and the French people for their coolness in the face of a new terrorist threat. Chirac later called a meeting of top ministers to discuss the government's response to the attack.
Juppe visited the wounded at the Kremlin-Bicetre hospital on Wednesday afternoon to express sympathy and to assure them of compensation.
Paris prosecutors said they had asked veteran anti-terrorist magistrates to start a judicial inquiry.
Police chiefs, Interior Minister Debre and Defence Minister Charles Millon called in riot police, gendarmes and troops to put a security operation codenamed Vigipirate back into force.

The plan, put in place during the 1995 bombings but gradually phased out, triggered patrols by police, paramilitary gendarmes and soldiers at public transport stations, public buildings and in the streets.
In a repeat of last year's precautions, commuters were urged to be on the lookout for abandoned packages while school officials were put on alert for suspiciously parked cars.

Paris police said they would remove or seal rubbish bins around schools, Metro stations, major shops, official buildings, tourist sites and other busy areas. Public toilets would be locked and markets and public squares would be put under increased surveillance.

The Foreign Ministry said protective measures were being reinforced at French diplomatic posts. A ministry spokesman said France had asked its European partners to step up their cooperation in the battle against terrorism.
In financial markets, meanwhile, shares in major French store groups fell on fears that the bomb attack would drive away shoppers in the weeks leading up to Christmas and New Year, brokers said.
After last year's attacks, dozens of suspected Moslem fundamentalists were rounded up and the government said it had destroyed the guerrilla network it blamed for those bombings.
